title: "The silent failures, one by one"
jupyter: python3

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import functools
import re
from _outils import *          # noqa: F403
ns = {"re": re}
for nom in ("MARK", "REDACTION", "protect", "restore"):
    exec(compile(source_de(nom, PARAGRAPHES), "<traduire_paragraphes>", "exec"), ns)
protect, restore = ns["protect"], ns["restore"]
```

This chapter is an inventory. Every problem that follows has one thing in common:
**none of them raises an error.** The program carries on, produces a plausible output,
and the fault shows up only when compared against the real text — or not at all.

That is the reason for the checks scattered through the code: version assertions,
redaction counts, counters of rejected segments, format-quality columns. Each one exists
because one of these cases got through.

## Overview

| # | what happens | what you observe | what catches it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | wrong architecture instantiated | fluent Croatian, unrelated to the source | version assertion, parameter count |
| 2 | the old splitting rejected short lines | "Croatian" corpus partly English | measuring the translated share |
| 3 | fixed `max_new_tokens` | end of long texts missing | `budget()` per batch |
| 4 | right padding in batched generation | plausible but mismatched outputs | `padding_side = "left"` |
| 5 | unmonitored out-of-memory | run stopped, found 2 h later | recursive re-splitting |
| 6 | redaction lost in translation | missing data manufactured | `restore`, per-note counter |
| 7 | `str.count("___")` over-counts | 3 false alarms | knowing how to read the signal |
| 8 | window too small | an F1 that measures tokenisation | window at 16384, `truncated_notes` |
| 9 | model that emits no JSON | looks like "always No" | `parse_failed` column |
| 10 | prescribed wording taken for an invention | the good models accused | `_ABSENCE_PHRASES` |
| 11 | `ij` as a substring | 21 false matches per note | word boundaries, case sensitivity |
| 12 | `pgrep -f` matches itself | GPU idle, job never launched | kill by explicit PID |
| 13 | a "4-bit" repo that is not | 39 GB instead of 19 | sum the file sizes on the Hub |
| 14 | call sized on the context window | 40 % of every note missing | size on the training length |
| 15 | model that copies instead of translating | perfect length ratio (0.997) | count the **language** of the output |

## 1. The checkpoint loaded under a different architecture

**Symptom.** HPLT, loaded with `transformers` 5.5.0, produces grammatical and fluent
Croatian, entirely uncorrelated with the source text. No warning.

**Cause.** The recent library picks a different model class for that configuration file,
randomly initialises the weights that do not exist in the checkpoint, and generates
plausible text out of nothing.

**The clue.** One log line: *110 M parameters* instead of 77 M.

**False lead.** Converting the checkpoint to `safetensors` — several hours lost. The
problem is the architecture instantiated, not the file format.

**Fix.** Pin the version, with an assertion that refuses to continue:

```python
assert (4, 26) <= (major, minor) <= (4, 30), (
    f"HPLT requires transformers 4.26-4.30, found {transformers.__version__}")
```

And always print the parameter count at load time. A version assertion is more useful
than a comment: it executes.

## 2. The "Croatian" corpus that stayed English {#sec-ancien-decoupage}

**Symptom.** A corpus announced as Croatian, 15.7 % of whose text had stayed in English
— and not just any part of it.

**Cause.** The first splitting classified lines with a rule along the lines of "at least
three words of three letters or more". `R IJ placement` contains only one, `placement`:
the line was therefore rejected and never translated. And that is exactly the shape of
the lines in the `Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure` section — that is, the place
where the catheter evidence the whole chain is looking for lives.

The extraction model, whose prompt is in English, was thus reading the most decisive
clues in their original language.

**What made it invisible.** The corpus *looked* like Croatian — 78.5 % of the text was.
And the bias ran in the direction of good news: it *improved* the Croatian F1, so
nothing pushed anyone to look for it.

**Fix, in two steps.** First widen the rule so that anything containing language gets
translated; then remove that line classification entirely in favour of paragraph
splitting, which has no rule to tune — see "The paragraph, a universal unit".

**Lesson.** A bias that flatters the result is more dangerous than a bug that degrades
it. And a rule that needs fine tuning is a rule that will eventually be tuned wrong.

## 3. The silent truncation of generation

**Symptom.** Long segments come back translated, but cut off mid-sentence. The CSV is
complete, the counters are satisfied.

**Cause.** A fixed `max_new_tokens=512`. The model stops at 512 tokens with nothing to
report it — it is not an error, it is the requested behaviour.

```{python}
budget = fonction("budget", PARAGRAPHES)
print("paragraph of 3300 characters:")
print(f"  tokens needed (~3.5 chars/token, +15 % in Croatian) : "
      f"~{int(3300 / 3.5 * 1.15)}")
print(f"  allowed by a fixed value of 512                     : 512  -> truncated")
print(f"  allowed by budget()                                 : "
      f"{budget(['x' * 3300])}")
```

**Fix.** Compute the ceiling per batch, from the longest segment.

## 4. Padding on the wrong side

**Symptom.** Batched generation on a decoder model: the outputs are grammatical but do
not correspond to the inputs.

**Cause.** With `padding_side="right"`, the last position of a short sequence is a
padding token. The model therefore continues *from the padding*, not from the end of the
prompt.

```
right padding:  [short prompt] [PAD] [PAD] <- the model continues here
left padding :  [PAD] [PAD] [short prompt] <- the model continues here
```

**Fix.** `tok.padding_side = "left"`. And as a bonus this makes stripping the prompt
trivial: every sequence in the batch has the same input length, so
`gen[:, enc["input_ids"].shape[1]:]` is valid for the whole batch.

## 5. The unmonitored out-of-memory

**Symptom.** A run launched, left alone, found stopped two hours later.

**Cause.** `batch_size=64` in bf16 on a note of 79 pieces. Within a batch, every
sequence is padded to the length of the longest: a 1,200-character piece forces its 63
neighbours up to that size.

**Recurrence.** The same failure came back later, at `--batch 24` on a 45 GB card: the
recursive re-splitting fired five times, then reached a batch of one element, where it
re-raises by design. The process died at note 78 of 125. The additional lesson: a
guardrail that bounds the damage does not replace correct sizing.

**Fix, in two steps.** Sort the batch by length — which removes the cause — and re-split
recursively on overflow — which bounds the consequence.

**Methodological lesson, the most expensive in the project.** Do not launch a run of
several hours without watching at least the first note.

## 6. The redaction lost in translation

**Symptom.** A Croatian note has one redaction fewer than its original. Nobody ever sees
it.

**Why it matters.** The opposite case is worse still: an *added* redaction manufactures
missing data where the source had text. It happened on the first note translated by hand
— `per AJ records` became `prema dokumentaciji ___`.

**Fix.** Three quarters of "Protecting what must not be translated": integer markers,
individual verification, and a per-note counter rather than silence.

```{python}
text, lost = restore("Bolesnica u 77701. godini, kateter od dr. 77703.", 3)
print(f"markers lost: {lost}  ->  reported in the CSV's `markers_lost`")
print("text:", text)
```

## 7. The counter that over-counts

**Symptom.** Three notes of the HPLT corpus flagged for a redaction mismatch. Two are
healthy.

**Cause.** `str.count("___")` counts two occurrences in `______`, whereas
`REDACTION = r"_{3,}"` sees — rightly — **one** redaction there, restored in its
canonical form.

```{python}
series = "grade ______ Abdomen"
p, n = protect(series)
back, _ = restore(p, n)
print(f"source  : count('___') = {series.count('___')}")
print(f"restored: count('___') = {back.count('___')}  (n = {n} marker)")
```

**Why not fix the counter.** Because a counter that over-reacts flags three notes of
which two are healthy: ten minutes of reading. A counter that under-reacts lets a real
loss through: a corpus. **An imperfect check biased the right way beats an accurate check
biased the wrong way.**

## 8. The window that measures tokenisation

**Symptom.** An F1 gap between English and Croatian, attributed to translation quality.

**Cause.** At `MAX_SEQ_LENGTH = 8192`, Croatian loses 7,547 tokens to truncation against
1,135 for English: a factor of 6.6. Croatian is less well represented in BPE
vocabularies, so it consumes more tokens for the same content.

**Fix.** A 16,384 window, where both corpora pass through whole. And count the truncated
notes in `comparison.csv`, so that the question does not come up again.

## 9. The model that emits no JSON

**Symptom.** A model shows a precision of 1.000.

**Cause.** One 31 B model failed to parse on 22 notes out of 40. Its precision covers 18
answers. Without the `parse_failed` column, a format failure and a "No" answer are
indistinguishable: both give `pred_catheter = False`.

**Fix.** Three format metrics beside the F1 — `parse_failed`, `no_evidence`,
`hallucinated_evidence` — and an immediate warning at the end of a run.

**Effect on the conclusions.** The model ranking changes. This is what turned format
quality into a first-class metric rather than a detail.

## 10. The hallucination detector that accuses the good models

**Symptom.** MedGemma 27B, which answers correctly 40 times out of 40, is flagged as
hallucinating on most of the negative cases.

**Cause.** The prompt **instructs** the model to write `no central venous device
documented` when nothing is documented. That sentence is not in the note, so the
detector counts it as invented. The more obedient the model, the more it is accused.

**Fix.** `_ABSENCE_PHRASES`, the list of wordings the prompt authorises.

**Lesson.** A checker has to know the rules given to the model, otherwise it measures
obedience backwards.

## 11. `ij` matches almost every Croatian word

**Symptom.** The abbreviation `IJ` is detected everywhere in the Croatian corpus.

```{python}
sentence = "Bolesnik koji je primljen prije tri dane, nije imao kateter."
print("substring 'ij':", len(re.findall("ij", sentence.lower())),
      re.findall(r"\w*ij\w*", sentence.lower()))
print("\\bIJ\\b, case-sensitive:", len(re.findall(r"\bIJ\b", sentence)))
```

**Fix.** Word boundaries, and case sensitivity for abbreviations — the word stems staying
case-insensitive to cover declension.

**Recurrence.** The same bug was reintroduced once, by an improvised command-line `grep`,
after having been fixed in the tool. **A fix that lives in a tool does not protect the
commands typed next to it.**

## 12. `pgrep -f` matches itself

**Symptom.** A wait loop meant to launch a job when another finishes never terminates.
The GPU sits idle throughout.

**Cause.** `pgrep -f "pattern"` finds its own command line, which contains the pattern.
The condition "the process is still running" is therefore always true.

**Made worse.** The corresponding `pkill` killed the shell that was running it — same
reason, opposite effect.

**Fix.** Get the PID explicitly (`ps -eo pid,cmd`), filter it, then act on that number.
Never on a pattern.

## 13. The "4-bit" repo that weighs twice as much

**Symptom.** `Qwen3-32B-unsloth-bnb-4bit` takes up 39 GB. `Qwen3-32B-bnb-4bit`, 19 GB.
Same model, same quantisation claim.

**Cause.** The first repo contains the unquantised weights *in addition to* the quantised
ones.

**Fix.** Never infer the size from the name: sum the file sizes through the Hub API
before downloading. It is the only reliable measurement, and it is free — one HTTP
request instead of 39 GB.

## 14. The call sized on the context window

**Symptom.** A 10,000-character note sent in one piece comes back translated into
impeccable English — but 40 % of the text is missing, always the end.

**Cause.** The model's context window (131,072 tokens) says what it can **read**, not
what it can **translate in one go**. That second figure is set by the length distribution
of its training data: sentence pairs. Beyond that, the model emits its end token and
**ignores the rest of the input**.

**What made it invisible.** No exception. The number of tokens produced was even well
under the allowed ceiling — 713 out of 1,985 — so nothing suggested a truncation.

**Fix.** Split by paragraph, a measured unit that is stable in both languages. Detail in
"The paragraph, a universal unit".

**What it cost.** Two complete runs. The intermediate strategy of filling up to 3,000
characters, which looked like a reasonable compromise, still lost 13 % of the redactions
and cut short 14 % of the notes — and it was **2.5 times slower** than fine-grained
splitting, because a batch generates until its longest sequence finishes.

## 15. The model that copies instead of translating

**Symptom.** Gemma 3 27B, on whole Croatian notes, returns outputs with length ratios of
0.997 and 0.995. Apparently perfect.

**Cause.** It was copying the Croatian. Out of 31 lines of content, 24 had stayed
Croatian. On a short text, the same model with the same prompt translated correctly — it
is the length that tipped it into "continue the pattern" mode.

**What made it invisible.** The check in place was the **length ratio**. A copy has a
ratio of 1.00: the metric could not, by construction, detect this case. That is the worst
kind of indicator — the one that gives its best score on the most serious failure.

**Fix.** A second check of nature rather than quantity: count the lines carrying marks of
the source language against those carrying marks of the target language.

**Lesson.** An indicator that cannot fail measures nothing. Before trusting a metric, you
have to know which failure it is incapable of seeing.

## What these fifteen cases have in common

Three traits, which suggest three habits:

**They produce a plausible output.** Fluent Croatian, valid JSON, a complete CSV. None of
them looks like a breakdown. Hence the first habit: *check the invariant, not the absence
of an error*. Count the redactions, count the parameters, count the parsing failures.

**Several flattered the result.** The partly-English corpus improved the Croatian F1; the
precision of 1.000 came from a sample shrunk by failures. Hence the second habit:
*suspect the good news first*.

**Four came from the verification tools themselves** — `_ABSENCE_PHRASES`, `\bport`, `ij`,
and the length ratio of case 15. Hence the third: *a checker is code, with bugs of its
own*. Re-read it against the real text, not against its intention.
